newsitem.title: USA: Texas' investments to bring in nearly $4 bln.
newsitem.headline: Texas' investments to bring in nearly $4 bln.

text.p: Texas' investments will bring in nearly $4 billion in interest and dividend earnings over the next two-year budget period, State Comptroller John Sharp announced Wednesday.
The $4 billion accounts for five percent of the state's total revenue during the 1998-99 biennium, a release from Sharp's office said.

"The rate of return on the state's four major public funds should at least keep pace with industry standards in the years ahead," Sharp said. "Even though interest rates are likely to remain below the historic highs of the early 1980s, the value of the state's major investment funds will help keep Texas in the black."

In the latest issue of his office's publication, Fiscal Notes, Sharp said the state's public portfolios are worth more than $81 billion, ranking Texas fourth in the nation for the total book value of its government-held cash and securities, behind California, New York and Ohio.

Texas' four major public funds--overseen by the Teacher Retirement System, Employees Retirement System, the Permanent School Fund, and the Permanent University Fund--account for more than 95 percent of the total value of state investments, the release said.
Sharp said the state's largest pool of public funds is entrusted to Teacher Retirement System, which held $50 billion in assets in 1996.
"Last year, the fund delivered $2 billion to almost 153,000 retired teachers or their families," he said.
The teacher fund gained $658 million in dividend income last year, while earning another $1.7 billion in interest and $2.9 billion from the sale of investments.

Texas' second largest public pension fund is held by Employees Retirement System, and is worth $13 billion. The fund netted $1.1 billion in investment income in fiscal 1996, and paid out $478 million in retirement benefits to former law enforcement officers, judges, elected officials, and state employees.

"Over the past two decades, TRS and ERS both have shifted their investments away from fixed-income securities toward a larger share of domestic and international stocks," Sharp said. "Today, about 60 percent of TRS investments and 46 percent of ERS investments are in stocks."
